extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century English readers interested in manners, morals, and social conduct (gentlemen and ladies)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive essays on social behaviour, breeding, and proper conduct (dress, speech, treatment of servants, clergy performance) aimed at improving public decorum and private virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and Plainness in Conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: The old English plainness and sincerity — honest disposition and straightforward speech — are true marks of greatness of mind and should be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the modern swollen dialect of vanity and compliment; do not practise hollow compliments or dissimulation. 'Words are like Money' (et verba valent ut nummi) only if they have intrinsic value; otherwise they are 'mere Cyphers'. Dissimulation brings perpetual inconvenience: it creates everlasting jealousy and suspicion so that a man is not believed when he speaks truth, nor trusted when he means honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Counterfeiting Virtue (Authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: To counterfeit or dissemble (to put on the appearance of a real excellency) is inferior to genuinely possessing that quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best way to seem anything is really to be what one would seem to be; keeping up a pretence is often more troublesome than possessing the virtue and is likely to be discovered, wasting all the pains taken to appear otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum (Regard to Decency) as Part of Good Breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Good breeding requires not transgressing the rule of life called Decorum — a regard to decency manifested in order, consistency, and moderation of words and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decency is concomitant to virtue and obtains approbation from others; negligence of what others think looks like arrogance or being abandoned. Distinguish virtues: e.g., justice never to do violence; modesty never to commit offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Gendered Dress and Behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: One should 'be themselves' and avoid adopting dress or airs inappropriate to one's sex; imitating foreign fashions that break natural character is a transgression of propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 'Amazonian' hunting-habit for ladies (petticoat with male habit) is awkward on English modesty; ladies should recommend themselves in dress, words, and actions as sister/daughter/wife rather than imitating masculine affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in Fashion and Avoidance of Vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive affectation in dress and carriage (swelled with vanity and compliment) undermines natural agreeableness and true esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fashion makes phrases and expressions of kindness cheap, the language runs into a lie; a return to plainness would restore the true value of compliments and mutual respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Pedantry and Intellectual Narrowness
rubrics_metrics.description: A pedant is anyone excessively confined to the knowledge of his own profession or particular way of life who cannot think outside that sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men-of-the-town, courtiers, soldiers, lawyers, state-pedants (wrapt up in news) are examples; shallow pedants praise one another and are vain. Prefer breadth: a learned man without common sense is insufferable; learning should finish good sense, not merely supply matter for impertinence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Learning with Common Sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning, like travelling, should perfect good sense; otherwise it makes a silly man ten thousand times more insufferable by giving him variety of matter for impertinence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book-pedant (one filled though confused with many books) is more supportable because he may yet give useful hints, but reading without taste or distinction is blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of an Effective Country Clergyman (Qualifications and Delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Country clergy should be of plain sense rather than showy learning, with a good aspect, a clear voice, a sociable temper, and some knowledge of popular pastimes (e.g., back-gammon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good elocution and graceful delivery are important; repeating excellent sermons with a handsome elocution is preferable to wasting spirits composing new laborious sermons — 'A Sermon repeated after this Manner, is like the Composition of a Poet in the Mouth of a graceful Actor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Divinity over Overlearned Compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the works of greater masters (e.g., Tillotson, Barrow, South) arranged into a natural series is preferable to clergy composing elaborate original discourses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digesting established sermons into a continued system of practical divinity is edifying and easier for the preacher and people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolent Management of Servants
rubrics_metrics.description: The general corruption of servants' manners is owing to the conduct of masters; good masters produce respectful, contented, and industrious servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat servants humanely and equally in temper; let orders be given kindly so they are received as favours; cultivate cheerfulness in performance of duty; occasion servants to appear without being driven away when master passes — this indicates affection and esteem rather than fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Rewarding and Advancement of Servants
rubrics_metrics.description: A good servant should be rewarded with opportunities for independence rather than mere cast-off clothes; settling a servant in a tenement, helping with apprenticeship, or enabling livelihood is the proper reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving old clothes (which create silly equality and mockery); help servants into independent livelihoods (practical manumission), since securing their children's futures and granting apprenticeships sustains diligence and loyalty across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality as the Foundation of Generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill of the purse (frugality) is the cardinal virtue enabling sustained generosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By practicing economy a master can spare larger, more meaningful rewards (e.g., paying fines, providing settlements) rather than only small trinkets; this produces lasting good rather than ephemeral favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitality and Courteous Reception of Neighbours
rubrics_metrics.description: Warm, sincere welcome of neighbours and guests (sharing produce, small useful gifts, polite correspondence) fosters good country sociability and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Will Wimble's small handmade presents (may-fly, angle-rods, garters) and Sir Roger's genuine welcome illustrate how low-cost, thoughtful acts maintain neighbourly bonds and personal reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a Well-Ordered Family and Long Tenure of Servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping long-serving, aged domestics and maintaining continuity in household staff reflects well on a master and fosters mutual affection and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stable household where servants grow old with a benevolent master produces manifest signs of content (tears at reunion, eager service) and demonstrates the master's humanity and good economy.
